note: In-session one-vendor panel under D154(b) as amended by D155, run on 2026-10-03 by a Claude Code orchestrating session (Claude Opus 5.5). Three panelists, each stance a separate set of contexts: institutionalist on claude-opus-5-5, bottom_up on claude-opus-5-5, wealth_sceptic on claude-sonnet-5-5, all Anthropic, each through Claude Code subagents. Each panelist answered in batches of 25 countries, one fresh context per batch and per round, so no context held two stances and none saw another panelist's text except the anonymised round-1 summary the round-2 prompt carries. Two rounds plus the indicator audit, at the code default scope (maxCoverage 0.5): 455 country-dimension cells across all 125 countries. Prompts are byte-identical to a gateway run's, built by pnpm bench delphi --in-session with prompt version 3; the system rules were given as a file each panelist read first. Every batch confirmed it read every prompt in full and wrote every answer by hand. No call failed and none was rerun into this file; an earlier attempt on prompt version 2 was discarded because panelists condensed prompts. One vendor means the spread measures stance, not vendor, and shared model-family blind spots are hidden by a narrow IQR (D155). An OpenAI panelist through the codex CLI (gpt-5.6-sol) can be added as a follow-up multi-vendor run, which supersedes this one under D155. Estimates are an interpretation layer beside the indicators and never enter score.

indicatorJudgements.rationale: Publication volume is an output of a research system funded by income, and says little about whether any organisation turns that knowledge into preparation for change. Correctly filed as an outcome, and weak on the construct.

A statistical office that produces timely, open and methodologically sound data is a durable institution of national sensing, which is the precondition for anticipation. It measures seeing the present rather than preparing for the future, and it tracks income less than most rows because several middle-income systems score well.

A mandated foresight function with continuity across governments is the institutional core of the dimension, provided the index scores mandate, budget line, link to decision cycles and survival across elections rather than mere existence of a unit. Existence alone is cheap and would be gamed by announcements.

Long-duration grant commitments reveal funder institutions willing to bind themselves to a horizon, which is a behavioural trace of anticipation. It sits closer to research policy design than to national preparation for change, and grant-length norms differ by funding tradition as well as by foresight.

Journal output counts only research that reaches indexed, mostly English-language formal channels, so it is an input to sensing capacity rather than a measure of it, and per-capita volume tracks university funding and income closely. It misses the applied, local and practitioner knowledge production that large middle-income countries rely on to read change.

The closest available measure of whether the state can see itself, and the SPI's design (openness, standards, data use) varies more independently of income than most series. It sees only the official statistical system and not distributed sensing by civil society, firms or local governments, so it understates countries where anticipation happens outside the centre.

A formal foresight unit is a plausible direct measure, but existence and mandate are easy to stage and say little about whether anyone acts on the signal; continuity is the stronger part. It also ignores anticipation done by subnational governments, communities and markets, so it should be read as one channel, not the capability.

Long grant horizons are a genuine behavioural signal of a funder willing to wait, and as a share it is less mechanically tied to income than spending levels. It is narrow: it covers only competitive public research funding, which is a small and formal slice of how a country prepares for change, and grant registers will be most complete in rich countries.

Article volume per head is a research-funding input that tracks income very closely and says little about whether a country identifies emerging change. It is an input, not a downstream outcome of anticipation.

The SPI measures the quality of the statistical system, which is a sensing input to anticipation rather than anticipation itself. Statistical capacity is heavily funded and correlates strongly with income, though it is a real institutional product.

A foresight function with mandate and continuity is the most direct behavioural measure of anticipation, and is not purchasable by wealth alone since poor and rich states both have or lack them. No data, so it cannot yet be tested.

Funder commitment to long horizons is a behaviour, and the share form removes the scale effect of spending. It is still only indirectly about anticipating change and, with no data, rests on an untested register.

The index combines survival, health and learning-adjusted schooling into expected productivity, which is a stock outcome of a school system and of income rather than a measure of how the country updates knowledge. The harmonised test-score component is the institutionally informative part, and the composite is among the most income-laden rows in the set.

Formal training inside firms is an organisational routine for distributing and updating knowledge, which fits the dimension, and it varies with firm size and sector more than with income. The skewed coverage toward middle-income countries means it cannot place the whole frame on one scale.

Participation in adult education is the most direct behavioural reading of continuous learning, and it reflects lifelong-learning institutions such as training funds and recognised providers. Its coverage is confined to rich members, and those systems are themselves funded by income.

Field-normalised citation share says whether a research system produces knowledge others use, which is acquisition at the frontier rather than national distribution or updating. Whole counting inflates small, internationally connected systems, so it partly measures collaboration networks rather than domestic research institutions.

The HCI is a stock outcome built from child survival, schooling and test scores, which tracks income per head very closely, and it describes the human capital a child inherits rather than how a country acquires and updates knowledge. It sees only formal schooling and none of the apprenticeship, peer and informal learning that carries skills in lower-income economies.

An observed act of organizations updating skills, with weak income loading, which is valuable. It counts only formal training in registered firms with permanent staff, so it misses informal apprenticeship, which is the main channel of workplace learning in much of Africa and South Asia.

Continuous adult learning is close to the construct, and including non-formal learning is the right instinct. Its sources exist only for OECD and European members, so as specified it would measure rich countries against each other and could not see community or informal learning elsewhere.

A field-normalized ratio is far better than raw volume and partly decoupled from income, but it measures the uptake of indexed academic research by the global research system, a narrow, English-weighted slice of how a country learns. Whole counting rewards co-authorship with large foreign systems, which says more about network position than domestic learning.

It combines child survival, schooling and test scores, a stock of health and education that follows income very closely. It reports what past spending produced, not how well a country updates knowledge now, so it is an outcome and not a direct capability measure.

A firm choosing to train staff is an observed act of knowledge acquisition and not obviously purchasable, and its income link in the middle-income sample is weak. It covers one actor type and the survey skips rich countries, so comparability is thin.

Continuing learning after school is the most direct behavioural sign of a country updating knowledge, but participation rises with income, service-sector jobs and funded provision. Only European and OECD data exist, so it cannot yet separate capability from wealth.

Citation share measures how elite research is used abroad, which follows funding, English-language reach and co-authorship with large systems, so wealth is a major driver. It captures a narrow slice of knowledge production and says little about distribution or updating at home.

Patent filings record experiments that cleared an expensive legal gate, and they reflect corporate R&D scale, filing strategy and subsidy regimes more than the ease of trying and abandoning approaches. They are also heavily concentrated in rich and large economies.

Trademarks are cheap and frequent, so they come closer to counting many small attempts at new products and firms, and they rely on an accessible IP office, which is an institutional precondition. They also count rebranding and defensive filings, and they partly duplicate design filings.

A design filing is a low-cost registered attempt at a new product form, but office routing distorts it badly: EU members file at EUIPO and the Netherlands at the Benelux office, so the cross-country reading partly measures where the registry sits. Subsidised filing inflates it elsewhere.

New repositories count cheap starts, but on one private platform whose reach depends on connectivity, language and the absence of domestic alternatives, and much of it is coursework rather than an attempt at a new approach. It says little about whether institutions let experiments be tested, abandoned and improved.

A count of first venture rounds captures attempts started with outside risk capital, which is close to the construct, and it relies on legal infrastructure for equity contracts and exits. It is an outcome of capital market depth that richer countries have, even counted by deal rather than amount.

TEA counts necessity self-employment the same as deliberate experiments, so it is high where formal labour markets fail rather than where trying is easy. From an institutional view that is individual effort compensating for institutional failure, and its wealth relation runs partly in reverse.

Stated fear of failure is an attitude toward the cost of abandoning an attempt, which is relevant, but the institutional substance is bankruptcy law, time to discharge and creditor recovery, which should be measured directly. Cultural response style is a large share of its variation.

Firms admitted to and exiting controlled regulatory trials is a direct trace of a state institution that lets new approaches be tried and ended under supervision, which is the dimension's question in institutional form. Counting completions as well as admissions is the right fix, though the measure is concentrated in finance and needs a common definition across regulators.

Spinouts are an output of technology transfer offices and IP rules that let researchers attempt commercialisation, which is relevant but narrow. Incompatible definitions and dependence on research university scale make it both hard to compare and income-laden.
The composition of R&D spending reflects ownership models and industrial structure rather than the ease of trying and abandoning approaches. Retirement is sound.

Patents count experiments only once they are formal, lawyered and filed, which excludes nearly all frugal and informal innovation in lower-income countries and is distorted by strategic and subsidised filing. It reads the size of a formal R&D system more than how easily new approaches are tried.

Cheaper and more frequent than patents, so closer to many small attempts, but it still counts only firms formal enough to register a mark. It partly duplicates industrial designs as a reading of formal product launches.

A registered product-form attempt is a plausible small experiment, but subsidy distortion, EUIPO leakage and the formal-filing filter make it a noisy reading that mostly repeats trademarks. Keep it only beside trademarks, not as an independent signal.

Zero-cost, no-registration attempts are exactly the kind of distributed experimentation formal registers miss, and developer communities in India, Nigeria, Brazil and Indonesia show up here. It still needs a computer and connectivity, counts coursework, and sees one platform, so it is a partial and access-loaded reading.

Counting first rounds rather than amounts is the right fix, but VC is a formal financing channel concentrated in rich hubs, and most new attempts in lower-income countries are funded by savings, family and community finance. It is an outcome of a financial ecosystem rather than a direct measure of attempting.

A household survey that counts formal and informal new businesses alike, so it is the one row here that sees people attempting things outside registers, and its inverse relation to income is a feature, not a flaw. Necessity entrepreneurship is still an attempt, though it says less about testing and abandoning than about trying.

Willingness to risk failure is central to the abandon-and-retry part of the construct, and the survey reaches informal would-be entrepreneurs. It is attitudinal with a restricted denominator, and cultural response styles shape it, so pairing it with an observed exit or restart measure would help.

Counting firms through sandboxes is a real observation of controlled trial and exit, but it captures only formal, mostly fintech firms dealing with sophisticated regulators. Lower-income countries experiment more through informal tolerance than through formal sandboxes, so this would understate them.

Spinouts measure commercialization from formal research universities, a narrow and income-loaded channel that says little about how easily people across the economy try new approaches. Definitional incompatibility makes it unusable anyway.
The composition of formal R&D spending is a structural input that reads ownership models and firm concentration, not experimentation. Retirement is right.

Patent filings per head follow R&D spending and legal sophistication, and reflect strategic filing and subsidy as much as experimentation. It records the surviving, expensive end of experiments, not how easily new approaches are tried and abandoned.

Trademarks mark branded commercial activity and rise with formal market size and legal capacity, so they mostly track income. They show launches of branded goods, which is only loosely experimentation.
Another IP filing count that partly duplicates trademarks, distorted by EUIPO routing, subsidised filing and a missing Netherlands series. Wealth and legal-system effects dominate.

Cheap, fee-free project starts are a good model of low-cost attempts, but they depend on connectivity, a developer workforce and platform access, all of which rise with income. Coursework, hubs and VPN misplacement add noise, and it covers one platform.

Counting first rounds is better than amounts, but a venture market is financial depth that rich countries have, so it tracks income and risk capital supply. It is an outcome of an ecosystem rather than a direct capability measure, and no data exists.

Many people trying to start businesses is behaviour and is not bought, and it runs higher in poorer countries partly from necessity self-employment. That inverse income pull makes it a poor wealth proxy but a muddy experimentation signal, and it is an outcome, not a capability.

Stated fear of failure is an attitude toward the cost of trying and abandoning, which is relevant to this construct. Self-reported, cross-cultural response differences matter, and the denominator is only people who see opportunities.

Firms passing through a regime built to allow trial and exit is the most direct observation of institutionalised experimentation here. Richer regulators run more sandboxes, so income and regulator capacity still matter. No data.

Spinouts depend on research budgets, technology transfer offices and finance, and definitions are incompatible across countries. A result of an academic ecosystem more than of ease of trying new approaches. No data.
It describes who performs research spending, not whether new approaches are attempted, and state ownership and single-firm dominance distort it. The retirement was sound.

The level of unemployment reflects the business cycle, informality and benefit design, and low rates in poor countries often mean no safety net rather than fast reallocation. It says little about response to change unless read as a path after a shock.

The share stuck in unemployment for a year or more is a better reading of whether labour market institutions move displaced people back into work, which is reallocation capacity. Its meaning flips in very tight markets, and survey design limits comparability, so it needs reading beside the rate.

Export concentration describes a product mix that resource endowment and specialisation set, which is a resilience-relevant outcome rather than a capacity to switch, so the C filing overstates it. High-value specialised exporters read as fragile when they are not.

Entry into new competitive export lines is observed reallocation of capital and labour, and the denominator avoids rewarding an already broad basket, so it fits the dimension well as an outcome. The 15-year window makes it slow, and resource finds count as adaptation.

Demonstrated preparation and recovery from shocks is the dimension's question applied to emergencies, and civil protection agencies, early warning and recovery bodies are exactly the institutions that should carry it. Available indices mix self-assessment and wealth-bought stocks, so the construct is valid but its realistic sources are not.

The speed at which rules and programmes are changed when conditions move, measured from legislative and regulatory timestamps, is the most direct institutional reading of adaptability in the list. Speed alone rewards churn and executive decree, so it should be paired with whether changes stick and are reviewed.

Where there is no unemployment insurance, people cannot afford to be unemployed and move into informal work, so low open unemployment in India or Indonesia reflects informal absorption rather than either rigidity or formal-sector fluidity. Ironically that absorption is a real adaptive capacity the row cannot distinguish from stagnation.

Duration is closer to reallocation speed than the level, but in economies with large informal sectors the measured unemployed are a selected, often educated urban group queuing for formal jobs, so the share reads queueing for formality as much as failure to adapt. The two-meanings problem in tight markets adds noise.

Basket concentration is a structural state, not a capacity to respond, filed as C but properly an outcome; it is heavily shaped by resource endowment and value-weighted lines. It sees formal merchandise trade only, missing the informal cross-border trade that is a large adaptive channel in Africa.

Entry into new lines is reallocation observed over time and normalized for room to enter, so it is the best row here and not strongly income-loaded. It only sees formal, recorded merchandise exports and moves over 15 years, so it misses quick domestic and informal pivots.

Recovery from a real shock is close to the construct, but available indices mix self-assessment and purchasable stocks, as the note says. A version built should observe community-level recovery (time for households, markets and local services to return), where much of the coping in lower-income countries actually happens.

Speed of rule and programme change is a direct capability reading in principle, but it measures only the formal state and would reward frequent rule-churn regardless of quality. It also misses that in many countries people adapt around slow formal rules rather than through them.

A modelled aggregate that mixes cycle, informality and labour market rules, and is high in some rich European states and low in poor informal economies. Weakly income-linked but also weakly about adaptability.
Persistence of joblessness hints at slow reallocation, but a small residual pool in tight markets reads the same way. Income link is moderate and survey coverage of long durations is uneven.

A basket composition outcome that rises with income and economic size, with the commodity exporters at the concentrated end. It reads a structure, not the ability to switch, so it is an outcome and not a direct capability measure.

Observed entry into new products is behaviour showing reallocation, and the rate is normalised by room to enter, which lowers the endowment effect. Poorer countries have more unexploited room and some rich ones less, so the income link is moderate; it remains goods only and an outcome.
The right construct, but every available proxy blends stocks of infrastructure and governance perception, so any real series would largely track income. No usable data.

Timestamped rule changes after shocks would directly show a system responding, and speed of change is not obviously bought. Cannot be assessed since nothing exists, and rule-change volume may also reflect instability.

It rates the democratic selection channel through expert opinion, which is one institutional route to a common project but not the capacity to see oneself in one, and it tracks income strongly. Retirement is justified.

A tax take is the fiscal contract made visible: citizens and firms collectively funding public goods through institutions they comply with, which is the institutional core of a common project. Central-government-only coverage misreads federations, resource rents distort it, and collection capacity rises with formality and income.

Inequality is a structural condition that constrains shared purpose rather than a measure of it, so it is better filed as an input than an outcome. Latin American and southern African countries dominate the bad end for historical and structural reasons, and income vs consumption survey bases differ across countries.

Belonging to the national community is adjacent to imagining a common project, but any attitudinal item risks rewarding nationalism and regime deference, which is why pride fails. Keeping it as a gap is right until an item passes the regime test.

Giving time to an organisation is observed behaviour of acting for others through institutions, which fits the dimension, though it partly reflects the density of the voluntary sector and religious traditions. It is self-reported, and it overlaps with charitable membership.

Hostile polarisation undermines the institutions through which plural actors can still act together, so it bears on the dimension, but as expert coding it cannot separate peaceful competition from suppressed opposition. Holding it as a check is correct.

Membership in charitable organisations is reported behaviour tied to organisations that persist beyond individuals, which an institutionalist values, and it does not appear inflated by state mass organisations. Membership is not activity, question format differs between EVS and WVS, and voluntary sector density rises with income.
An expert perception of the formal democratic channel, which is one route into a common project but not the capacity to see oneself in it, and it tracks income strongly. Retirement is right.

Central tax take reads fiscal structure, federalism, resource rents and the size of the formal economy that can be taxed, so a country where most work is informal reads low whatever people contribute. It ignores the community levies, zakat, harambee and mutual-aid contributions through which many people fund shared goods.

Inequality is a structural condition that may constrain a common project, so it is an input rather than an outcome of the capability, and highly unequal societies can still sustain strong collective projects. Gini also mixes income and consumption surveys across countries, which weakens comparability.

Belonging is adjacent to the construct, but identification with the nation is not the same as participation in a common project, and local, ethnic or religious communities are often where collective action actually lives. Keeping it a gap until a regime-neutral item exists is right.

Giving time is a direct behaviour of participating in shared projects, and broad definitions reach informal helping; low-income countries such as Indonesia and Kenya have read high on this kind of item. It should count informal volunteering, not only time given to an organization, or it undercounts community self-help.

Hostile polarization does erode the capacity for collective action, but expert coding of elite camps says little about cooperation among ordinary people and reads calm in regimes with no opposition. Keeping it as an unscored check is right.

Membership in charitable organizations is the best wired row because it is a reported behaviour toward strangers, but it counts formal organizations and so misses informal mutual-aid groups, burial societies and neighbourhood associations, and question-format differences add spread. Membership is also not activity.
It measures the democratic channel as seen by experts, correlating with income and regime type, and not whether people see themselves in a common project. Singapore shows the construct mismatch.

Tax take rises strongly with income and with state formalisation, and is confounded by resource rents and federal accounting. It is an outcome of fiscal capacity more than willingness to fund a common project.

A structural condition that may constrain belonging but is not a measure of it, and the sign is contested because redistribution and market inequality differ. Its income link is moderate and non-monotonic, and survey comparability is patchy.
Belonging is the closest construct, and the self-report is not wealth bound, though autocracies inflate attachment items. No usable series exists, and pride proxies must not stand in for it.

Giving time to others is behaviour acted on, and is quite weakly related to income, with some poor countries high. Self-report, informal helping outside organisations, and proprietary data limit it; no data.

Hostile division is relevant, but pluralism is the target and calm can mean suppression, so the direction is ambiguous. Expert-coded and the benchmark has no way yet to separate calm from repression. No data.

Reported membership of charitable bodies is a behaviour aimed at strangers and is robust to state mass organisations. It rises with income through associational infrastructure, and survey format and membership versus activity weaken it.
